name: Writing Support
title: Writing Support
answer: Writing support for English learners uses AI as a language resource while the student does the writing, with the teacher shaping when and how the tool and the student's home language are used together. It matters because the benefit comes from teacher mediation rather than the tool alone, and because the same fade principle that applies to translation should apply here so students gradually depend on the tool less.

sections.body: Writing in a new language is demanding, and AI can help with it only when a teacher shapes how it is used. The idea is that a student might brainstorm in their home language and then write in English while the tool offers help on particular words or structures. Throughout, the student remains the writer and the tool serves as a language resource rather than a replacement. Over time the student relies on the tool less, following the same fade principle as translation. This solves the problem of AI being handed over without guidance, which loses the mediation that makes it work.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a secondary classroom, a bilingual writing routine might begin with brainstorming in the home language, followed by writing in English with the tool assisting on specific words or structures. Students are taught when and how to combine their home language and the AI, so the pairing is planned rather than incidental. The teacher's role is to mediate that use, deciding where the tool helps and where the student works unaided. The text does not give grade band variations beyond the secondary students in the study and the teachers observed across the United States. The same fade principle as translation applies, so support is withdrawn as the student's own writing grows.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with research evidence. In a study of 48 immigrant secondary students learning Spanish, generative AI used with teacher guidance and planned use of students' home languages improved academic literacy, pronunciation, and motivation over eight weeks (de Amo Sanchez-Fortun, 2026). The text states that the key was teacher mediation, not the tool alone, and that students were taught when and how to use their home language and the AI together. Separately, observations of 42 teachers found them using ChatGPT to communicate with multilingual learners, differentiate materials, and build scaffolds (Donley, 2024). The same study noted gaps in how teachers used AI for assessment and reflection.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets teacher mediation as the central limit: the tool alone did not produce the gains, and students had to be taught when and how to combine their home language with the AI. The student must do the writing, with the tool acting only as a language resource, and reliance on it should decrease over time through the fade principle. The observed gaps in teachers' use of AI for assessment and reflection are flagged as worth attention, since assessment is where errors cause the most harm. Those decisions about use, fading and assessment stay with the teacher rather than the tool.
